{{context|date=December 2015}}

In statistics, '''jackknife variance estimates for random forest''' are a way to estimate the [[variance]] in [[random forest]] models, in order to eliminate the [[Bootstrapping (statistics)|bootstrap]] effects.

==Jackknife variance estimates==
The sampling variance of bagged learners is:
:<math>V(x) = Var[\hat{\theta}^{\infty}(x)]</math>
Jackknife estimates can be considered to eliminate the bootstrap effects. The jackknife variance estimator is defined as:<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wager|first1=Stefan|last2=Hastie|first2=Trevor|last3=Efron|first3=Bradley|title=Confidence Intervals for Random Forests: The Jackknife and the Infinitesimal Jackknife|journal=Journal of Machine Learning Research|date=2014-05-14|volume=15|issue=1|pages=1625–1651|pmid=25580094|pmc=4286302|arxiv=1311.4555|bibcode=2013arXiv1311.4555W}}</ref>
:<math>\hat{V}_j = \frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat\theta_{(-i)} - \overline\theta)^2</math>
In some classification problems, when random forest is used to fit models, jackknife estimated variance
is defined as:
:<math>\hat{V}_j = \frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\overline t^{\star}_{(-i)}(x) - \overline t^{\star}(x))^2</math>
Here, <math>t^{\star}</math>denotes a decision tree after training, <math>t^{\star}_{(-i)}</math> denotes the result based on samples without <math>ith</math> observation.

==Examples==
[[Email spam|E-mail spam]] problem is a common [[Classification problem (mathematics)|classification problem]], in this problem, 57 features are used to classify spam e-mail and non-spam e-mail. Applying IJ-U variance formula to evaluate the accuracy of models with m=15,19 and 57. The results shows in paper( Confidence Intervals for Random Forests: The jackknife and the [[Infinitesimal]] Jackknife ) that m = 57 random forest appears to be quite unstable, while predictions made by m=5 random forest appear to be quite stable, this results is corresponding to the evaluation made by error percentage, in which the accuracy of model with m=5 is high and  m=57 is low.

Here, [[Accuracy and precision|accuracy]] is measured by error rate, which is defined as:
:<math>Error Rate = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{M}y_{ij},</math>
Here N is also the number of samples, M is the number of classes, <math>y_{ij}</math> is the [[indicator function]] which equals 1 when <math>ith</math> observation is in class j, equals 0 when in other classes. No probability is considered here. There is another method which is similar to error rate to measure accuracy:
:<math>logloss = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{M}y_{ij}log(p_{ij})</math>
Here N is the number of samples, M is the number of classes, <math>y_{ij}</math> is the indicator function which equals 1 when <math>ith</math> observation is in class j, equals 0 when in other classes. <math>p_{ij}</math> is the predicted probability of <math>ith</math> observation in class <math>j</math>.This method is used in [[Kaggle]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kaggle.com/c/otto-group-product-classification-challenge/details/evaluation|website=Kaggle|accessdate=|title=Otto Group Product Classification Challenge }}</ref>
These two methods are very similar.

==Modification for bias==
When using [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo]] MSEs for estimating <math>V_{IJ}^{\infty}</math> and <math>V_{J}^{\infty}</math>, a problem about the Monte Carlo bias should be considered, especially when n is large, the bias is getting large:
:<math>E[\hat{V}_{IJ}^B]-\hat{V}_{IJ}^{\infty}\approx\frac{n\sum_{b=1}^{B}(t_b^{\star}-\bar{t}^{\star})^2}{B}</math>
To eliminate this influence, bias-corrected modifications are suggested:
:<math>\hat{V}_{IJ-U}^B= \hat{V}_{IJ}^B - \frac{n\sum_{b=1}^{B}(t_b^{\star}-\bar{t}^{\star})^2}{B}</math>
:<math>\hat{V}_{J-U}^B= \hat{V}_{J}^B - (e-1)\frac{n\sum_{b=1}^{B}(t_b^{\star}-\bar{t}^{\star})^2}{B}</math>
